About: the main-sequence turn-off of a star cluster and how it measures the cluster's age

About this simulation

On screen
A Hertzsprung–Russell diagram of 27 stars of one age, luminosity L upwards from 10−2 to 106 L⊙ and effective temperature across from 40 000 K at the left to 3000 K at the right, both logarithmic. Each star is a glowing dot in the colour of a blackbody at its temperature; a star that has left the main sequence is a faint grey ring at the place it held. The main-sequence line is solid below the turn-off and dotted above it; the accent dot marks the turn-off and the open ring marks the one-solar-mass star. The inset plots the main-sequence lifetime against the mass, with a line at the present age and a reference line at the age of the Universe.
Controls
The age slider sets the cluster's age from 106 to 1.3 × 1010 years on a logarithmic scale and pauses the run. ▶ Play raises the age by one decade every 8 s and stops at 1.3 × 1010 years.
Measured
Mto is the mass whose main-sequence lifetime equals the age, Lto the luminosity of a main-sequence star of that mass, and a star counts as on the main sequence while its lifetime exceeds the age. Mto is shown to two decimal places and Lto to three significant figures.
Assumptions
Every star follows the same rough power laws: L = L⊙ (M/M⊙)3.5, R = R⊙(M/M⊙)0.8 and a main-sequence lifetime of 1010 years × (M/M⊙)−2.5. They are good to a factor of about two near the Sun; real massive stars shine less steeply and so live longer than this rule gives (none lives less than about 3 million years). A star that leaves the main sequence becomes a giant and then a white dwarf or a remnant; those phases are not drawn.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Who leaves first

Set the age of the cluster to 106 years, so that every star is still on the main sequence. Before raising the age, predict which stars will be the first to leave the main sequence.

2 · Lifetime of a heavy star

Set the age to 107 years. A star of 10 M⊙ has ten times as much hydrogen as the Sun and is about 3000 times as luminous. Before raising the age until the turn-off mass reads 10 M⊙, predict how its main-sequence lifetime compares with the Sun's lifetime of 1010 years.

3 · Turn-off mass as the cluster ages

Set the age to 108 years, about the age of the Pleiades, and read the turn-off mass. Before raising the age tenfold, to 109 years, predict how the turn-off mass will change.

4 · Turn-off brightness as the cluster ages

Set the age back to 108 years and read the turn-off luminosity. Before raising the age to 109 years again, predict how the turn-off luminosity will change.

5 · The oldest clusters

Keep the age at 109 years from question 4. Before raising it to 1.3 × 1010 years, the age of the oldest globular clusters, predict where the turn-off will then lie and which stars will still be on the main sequence, and then raise it.

6 · What you found

A cluster's stars are born together, so they differ only in mass. The heaviest leave the main sequence first, and the turn-off, where the lifetime equals the age, moves down the line as the cluster ages.

With a lifetime of about 1010 years × (M/M⊙)−2.5, the turn-off mass falls as t−0.4 and its luminosity as t−1.4, so reading the turn-off gives the cluster's age.

The oldest globular clusters, at about 1.3 × 1010 years, turn off just below the Sun: near 0.9 M⊙ in this simple model, nearer 0.8 M⊙ in real metal-poor globular clusters.

01

At a glance

The stars of a cluster formed together, so they share one age and differ only in mass. This sim sets that age and shows, on a Hertzsprung–Russell diagram of 27 stars, which of them are still on the main sequence, and what the end of that sequence tells you about the cluster.

What you'll learn

  • What sets how long a star stays on the main sequence.
  • How the turn-off, the end of the main sequence, depends on the cluster's age.
  • How a cluster's age is read from its turn-off.
The opening state: all 27 stars on the line, the Sun ringed, the pink turn-off marker above the top of it.

What's on screen

  • Glowing dot: one star, in the colour of a blackbody at its temperature. Luminosity L rises up the page, temperature falls from left to right.
  • Pink dot: the turn-off. Open ring: the Sun. Faint grey ring: a star that has left the main sequence, drawn where it stood.
  • Inset and readouts: the inset plots main-sequence lifetime against mass, with a pink line at the cluster's age. The readouts give the age, then the turn-off's mass and luminosity, and how many stars remain on the main sequence.
See itLook at the opening age, 106 yr. Watch for: every star drawn as a bright dot, Stars on main sequence reading 27 of 27, and the pink marker above the top of the line.

03

Heavier stars live shorter: the fuel grows as M, the burning as M3.5

A star lives on the main sequence by burning core hydrogen, so its life is fuel divided by burn rate: tMS ∝ M/L (notes 4.78). With the observed L ∝ M3.5, and the same burned fraction for every star, the notes get (4.79):

Equation (4.79). tMS,⊙ = 1010 yr is the Sun's main-sequence lifetime.
Lifetime against mass, as in the sim's inset. Mass runs from high at the left to low at the right.

Ten times the Sun's mass is ten times the fuel but 103.5 ≈ 3000 times the luminosity, so the life is shorter by 102.5 ≈ 300, about 3 × 107 yr. The faintest star in the sim, 0.52 M⊙, would last 5 × 1010 yr, longer than the age of the Universe.

Key idea. A star is on the main sequence while its lifetime exceeds the cluster's age. The bright, blue, high-mass stars have the shortest lives, so they are the first to fall short.
See itSet the age to 3.16 × 107 yr, the lifetime of a 10 M⊙ star. Watch for: the stars above the pink dot drawn as grey rings, and Mass reading 10.00 M⊙.
04

The turn-off mass falls as the cluster ages, Mto ∝ t−0.4

At age t, every star whose lifetime is shorter than t has left. The main sequence therefore ends at the mass whose lifetime equals t: the turn-off mass Mto, the sim's Mass readout. Inverting (4.79) gives (4.80):

Equation (4.80). The turn-off is the point on the line occupied by stars of this mass.

Each tenfold rise in age lowers Mto by 100.4 ≈ 2.5, not by ten. The sim's 27 stars thin out accordingly:

age tMto (M⊙)on the main sequence
108 yr6.3116 of 27
109 yr2.5110 of 27
1.3 × 1010 yr0.904 of 27

At 1.3 × 1010 yr the turn-off lies just below the Sun. In this model only stars lighter than about 0.9 M⊙ live that long; real metal-poor globular clusters turn off nearer 0.8 M⊙.

See itWatch the age rise from 108 to 109 yr. Watch for: Mass falling from 6.31 to 2.51 M⊙, the pink dot sliding down the line, and Stars on main sequence going from 16 to 10.
05

The turn-off dims faster than its mass falls, Lto ∝ t−1.4

With L ∝ M3.5, the luminosity at the turn-off follows from (4.80), as (4.81):

Equation (4.81), the sim's Luminosity readout.

That is 101.4 ≈ 25 per decade of age, against 2.5 for the mass. From 108 to 109 yr, Mto goes from 6.3 to 2.5 M⊙ while Lto goes from about 630 to 25 L⊙. Turned round, it gives the age from the turn-off's luminosity (4.82):

Equation (4.82). Since −5/7 is the inverse of −1.4, this is (4.81) solved for t.
log t

This slider moves the sim's age slider too.

See itWatch the age rise from 107 to 109 yr. Watch for: Luminosity falling about 630-fold, from 1.58 × 10⁴ to 25.1 L⊙, while Mass falls only about 6-fold.
06

Where it matters

  • Dating clusters. The Pleiades, about 108 yr old, turn off near 6.3 M⊙; the Hyades, about 6 × 108 yr, near 3.1 M⊙. The oldest globular clusters, between about 1.2 and 1.3 × 1010 yr, turn off just below the Sun, near 0.8 M⊙. Since the Galaxy cannot be younger than its oldest stars, their ages set a lower limit on its age.
  • The giant branches. Stars above the turn-off are on the subgiant and giant branches, which are brief next to the main-sequence life, so their masses are only slightly above Mto. The sim shows those stars only as grey rings.
  • Very young clusters. Low-mass stars take longest to contract onto the main sequence (the Kelvin–Helmholtz time), so a cluster a few million years old has an incomplete lower end. The sim does not draw this.
Go deeper: how far to trust the power laws
  • L ∝ M3.5 and tMS ∝ M−2.5 are good to about a factor of two near the Sun. Real massive stars shine less steeply, so they live longer than the rule says: none lives less than about 3 million yr, so the sim's left-hand end is idealised.
  • In practice astronomers fit isochrones computed from stellar models. The age from luminosity also needs the cluster's distance, since L comes from apparent brightness by the inverse-square law.
See itSet the age of the oldest globular clusters, 1.3 × 1010 yr. Watch for: the pink dot just below the Sun's ring, Mass reading 0.90 M⊙, and 4 of 27 stars still on the main sequence.
07

Summary

In one line. A cluster's stars share one age and differ only in mass, so the turn-off, where the main-sequence lifetime equals that age, is the marker from which the age is read.

Key points

  • tMS ∝ M−2.5: the fuel grows as M, but the burn rate L grows as M3.5.
  • The turn-off mass is Mto = M⊙ (t / tMS,⊙)−0.4, and stars heavier than it have left.
  • The turn-off luminosity falls faster, Lto ∝ t−1.4, so Lto gives the age (and needs the distance).
  • The power laws are rough; real ages come from isochrone fits.

Common mix-ups

  • "The faint stars leave first, because they have the least fuel." They also burn far more slowly. L grows faster than the fuel, so the bright upper-left stars leave first.
  • "Ten times the mass means ten times the lifetime." It means ten times the fuel and about 3000 times the luminosity, so the life is about 300 times shorter.
  • "A cluster as old as the globulars has no main sequence left." Stars below about 0.9 M⊙ in this model (about 0.8 M⊙ in real globular clusters) live longer than 1.3 × 1010 yr, so they are still on it.

Things to try on your own

  • Set log t to 10.00, the Sun's lifetime, and compare the pink dot with the ring that marks the Sun.
  • Press Play and note Stars on main sequence as the age passes 107, 108 and 109 yr.
  • Find the age at which Mass reads 3.00 M⊙, then check it against (4.80).
